title: Independence and bases
objectives: Test vectors for independence and choose a basis.
Read the dimension of a space as the size of any basis.

screens.title: Spare arrows
screens.prose: Three arrows in the plane: $\mathbf{u} = (2, 1)$, $\mathbf{v} = (1, 3)$ and $\mathbf{w} = (3, 4)$.
screens.question: Tap every arrow that is a combination of the other two.

hints.text: Add $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$. What do you get?
$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$. Now rearrange that equation.
$\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w} - \mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w} - \mathbf{u}$.

feedback.correct: Each arrow can be built from the other two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one relation between the three arrows, then rearrange it.

explain.text: The parallelogram shows $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w}$. Move terms across and each arrow is built from the other two. One of the three is always spare.

screens.title: Back to the origin
screens.prose: The sliders set weights $c_1$, $c_2$ and $c_3$. The arrows chain $c_1\mathbf{u}$, then $c_2\mathbf{v}$, then $c_3\mathbf{w}$, head to tail.
screens.question: Which weights, not all zero, bring the chain back to the origin?

options.why: That always works and tells us nothing. We want weights that are not all zero.
Adding all three goes out to $(6, 8)$. $\mathbf{w}$ has to come back, so its weight is negative.
That ends at $(2 - 1 + 3, 1 - 3 + 4) = (4, 2)$. It is $\mathbf{w}$ that undoes $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$.

hints.text: Recall $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$. Which weight undoes the trip out along $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set each pair of weights on the sliders and watch where the chain ends.

explain.text: With weights $(1, 1, -1)$ the chain goes out along $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, then $-\mathbf{w}$ brings it home. A combination giving $\mathbf{0}$ with weights not all zero means one vector is spare. Such vectors are **dependent**.

screens.title: Independent or dependent
screens.prose: Vectors are **independent** when the only combination giving $\mathbf{0}$ has every weight zero. Otherwise they are **dependent**. Here $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1)$, $\mathbf{b} = (-4, -2)$ and $\mathbf{c} = (1, 2)$.
screens.question: Which pair is dependent?

options.why: $c_1(2, 1) + c_2(1, 2) = \mathbf{0}$ forces $c_1 = c_2 = 0$. They point in different directions, so they are independent.
$\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ point in different directions. No non-zero weights cancel them.

hints.text: Look for two arrows on the same line through the origin, even if they point opposite ways.
Compare $\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{a}$.
$\mathbf{b} = -2\mathbf{a}$, so $2\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a pair with non-zero weights that cancel.

explain.text: $\mathbf{b} = -2\mathbf{a}$ points the opposite way along the same line. Weights $(2, 1)$ give $2\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, so the pair is dependent. Opposite directions still count as one line.

screens.title: Testing by elimination
screens.prose: In 3D we cannot eyeball it. Put the vectors $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 0, 1)$ in the columns of $\mathbf{A}$. Then $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c}$ is the combination with weights $\mathbf{c}$, and we eliminate.
screens.question: How many pivots does elimination find?

hints.text: A pivot is the first non-zero entry in a row, after elimination.
Look at row 3 after elimination.
Rows start with 1, 1 and 2, in columns 1, 2 and 3.

feedback.correct: Three pivots, one in every column.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rows that keep a non-zero entry after elimination.

byKey.two: Row 3 ends as $(0, 0, 2)$, not all zeros. Its 2 is a third pivot.

explain.text: Every column has a pivot, so there is no free variable. Then $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ forces $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$: the nullspace is just $\mathbf{0}$. So the three vectors are independent.

screens.prose: Back to the plane. Put $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ from the start into the columns of a $2 \times 3$ matrix. The same would hold for any three vectors in the plane.
screens.question: At most how many pivots can elimination find in a $2 \times 3$ matrix?

widget.label: Most pivots possible
widget.accept: 2: at most one pivot per row.

hints.text: Each pivot sits in its own row.
Count the rows.
Two rows, so at most two pivots. One of the three columns must miss out.

feedback.correct: Two rows allow two pivots, so one column is always free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pivots need separate rows as well as separate columns.

byKey.per-col: You expected one pivot per column. Each pivot also needs its own row, and there are only two rows.

explain.text: With two rows there are at most two pivots, so one column is free. A free variable gives a non-zero $\mathbf{c}$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$. Three vectors in the plane are always dependent.

screens.prose: Three vectors in 3D: $\mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 2, 3)$, $\mathbf{a}_2 = (4, 5, 6)$ and $\mathbf{a}_3 = (7, 8, 9)$. No two of them are parallel.
screens.question: Are they independent?

options.text: Yes. No two of them are parallel.
options.why: You checked pairs only. Dependence can need all three at once: $\mathbf{a}_1 - 2\mathbf{a}_2 + \mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf{0}$.
Check it: $\mathbf{a}_1 + \mathbf{a}_2 = (5, 7, 9)$, not $(7, 8, 9)$. Eliminate to find the real relation.

hints.text: Eliminate and count the pivots.
Then $R_3 - 2R_2$ is all zeros. Column 3 has no pivot.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run elimination and look for a column without a pivot.

byKey.pairwise: You checked pairs only. Dependence can need all three at once: $\mathbf{a}_1 - 2\mathbf{a}_2 + \mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf{0}$.

explain.text: Elimination leaves row 3 all zeros, so column 3 has no pivot. Setting $c_3 = 1$ gives $c_2 = -2$ and $c_1 = 1$: $\mathbf{a}_1 - 2\mathbf{a}_2 + \mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf{0}$. Pairwise checks miss relations among three.

screens.title: A basis
screens.prose: A **basis** is a set of independent vectors that spans the space. Here $\mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = (1, -1)$ redraw the grid. Every point is one combination of them.
screens.question: Which weights give $\mathbf{p} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + c_2\mathbf{b}_2$?

options.why: Those are the coordinates of $\mathbf{p}$ on the usual grid. $3(1, 1) + 1(1, -1) = (4, 2)$.
$1(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (3, -1)$. You swapped the weights.

hints.text: Write it out: $c_1 + c_2 = 3$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 1$.
Count steps along the skewed grid lines from the origin to $\mathbf{p}$.
Add the two equations: $2c_1 = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $c_1 + c_2 = 3$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 1$.

explain.text: $c_1 + c_2 = 3$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 1$ give $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = 1$. On the skewed grid $\mathbf{p}$ sits two steps along $\mathbf{b}_1$ and one along $\mathbf{b}_2$. Because the basis is independent, no other weights work.

screens.question: Which set is a basis for the plane?

options.why: $\mathbf{s} = -\mathbf{p}$. They lie on one line, so they span only that line.
These span the plane, but $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}$. A basis has no spare vector.
One vector spans a line, not the plane.

hints.text: A basis must span the plane and have no spare vector.
Two of the arrows lie on one line. One arrow is the sum of two others.
$\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ point in different directions, and nothing in the set is spare.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are independent and span the plane.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each set: does it span the plane, and is any vector spare?

explain.text: $\{\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}\}$ spans the plane with nothing spare. Every basis of the plane has exactly two vectors. That count is the **dimension**: the plane has dimension 2.

screens.prose: Vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ are independent when $$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0} \implies c_1 = \cdots = c_n = 0.$$ To test, put them in the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ and eliminate. Independent means a pivot in every column. A basis is independent and spans. Its size is the dimension.
screens.question: You have four vectors in 3D. What can you say before computing anything?

options.text: They are independent if no two are parallel
options.why: Pairwise checks miss relations among three or four. A $3 \times 4$ matrix has at most 3 pivots, so one column is free.

options.text: They could be a basis of 3D
options.why: A basis of 3D has exactly 3 vectors. Four is one too many to be independent.

feedback.correct: Three rows allow at most three pivots, and there are four columns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the most pivots a $3 \times 4$ matrix can have.

explain.text: Put the four vectors in a $3 \times 4$ matrix. Three rows give at most three pivots, so one column is free and a non-zero combination gives $\mathbf{0}$. More vectors than entries always means dependent.

screens.title: A redundant factor
screens.prose: You regress a fund’s daily returns on three factors: large caps $L$, small caps $S$, and the size spread $\text{SMB} = S - L$. Two analysts fit the same data with identical fitted returns. One reports loadings $(0.6, 0.4, 0)$ on $(L, S, \text{SMB})$.
screens.question: The other analyst reports 0.8 on $L$ and 0.2 on $S$. What is their loading on SMB?

hints.text: Write the second fit as $0.8L + 0.2S + k(S - L)$ and match it to $0.6L + 0.4S$.
Match the $L$ terms: $0.8 - k = 0.6$.
Then $k = 0.2$. Check the $S$ terms: $0.2 + k = 0.4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand SMB as $S - L$ and match the $L$ and $S$ terms.

byKey.sign: With $-0.2$ the $L$ term is $0.8 + 0.2 = 1.0$. SMB adds $-L$, so a positive loading lowers $L$.
byKey.unique: You assumed the loadings are unique. Since SMB $= S - L$, different loadings can give the same fit.

explain.text: SMB is a combination of $L$ and $S$, so the three factor columns are dependent. Adding $k$ to SMB and moving $k$ from $S$ to $L$ leaves every fitted return unchanged. The regression cannot separate them, so drop one factor.

canvas.caption: SMB = S − L on every day

ideas: Vectors are independent when the only combination giving $\mathbf{0}$ has every weight zero.
Test by elimination: put the vectors in columns. Independent means a pivot in every column.
A basis is an independent set that spans. Every basis of a space has the same size, its dimension.

formula.name: Independence
formula.note: More vectors than entries always means dependent.

summary.trap: Checking pairs is not enough. $(1, 2, 3)$, $(4, 5, 6)$ and $(7, 8, 9)$ are pairwise non-parallel, yet dependent.

options.text: Yes: they point in opposite directions
options.why: Opposite directions lie on the same line. $3(1, 2) + (-3, -6) = \mathbf{0}$.

options.text: Yes: neither is the zero vector
options.why: Non-zero vectors can still be dependent when one is a multiple of the other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for non-zero weights that cancel the pair.

explain.text: $(-3, -6) = -3(1, 2)$, so $3(1, 2) + (-3, -6) = \mathbf{0}$ with non-zero weights. The two vectors lie on one line, so they are dependent.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $(3, k)$ must be a multiple of $(1, 2)$.

byKey.add: You added 3 to 2. Dependence needs a multiple: $(3, k) = 3(1, 2)$.
byKey.flip: You divided 3 by 2. The first entry triples, so the second must too: $k = 3 \times 2$.

explain.text: Dependent here means $(3, k)$ is a multiple of $(1, 2)$. The first entry is 3 times bigger, so $k = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

options.why: Each vector has three entries, but the dimension counts basis vectors, not entries.
The two special solutions are independent: each has a 1 where the other has a 0.

feedback.correct: Two independent special solutions span it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the vectors in a basis of the nullspace.

explain.text: The special solutions span $N(\mathbf{A})$, and they are independent. So they form a basis with two vectors: the nullspace is a plane, of dimension 2.

quiz.prose: Four candidate sets in the plane.
quiz.question: Which one is a basis for the plane?

options.why: Any set holding $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent: $5 \cdot \mathbf{0} + 0 \cdot (1, 0) = \mathbf{0}$ with a non-zero weight.
These span the plane, but $(1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1)$ is spare.
$(2, 4) = 2(1, 2)$, so they span only a line.

feedback.correct: Two independent vectors in the plane.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A basis of the plane has two independent vectors.

explain.text: $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ point in different directions, so they are independent and span the plane. The zero vector makes any set dependent, so it never belongs to a basis.
